To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

three ionic currents, a TTX-sensitive sodium current, a 4AP-sensitive potassium current, and a T/R-type calcium current, contribute to the pacemaker oscillations of Pn neurons, and that these currents are potential targets for steroid regulation of the sexually dimorphic Eod frequency in the brown ghosts knifefish, A. leptorhynchis.

the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin initially reduced spike frequency of pacemaker neurons and then reduced spike amplitudes and stopped pacemaker firing, the potassium channel blocker 4-aminopridine increased pacemaker firing frequency by approximately 20%, and the nonspecific calcium channel blocker cadmium reduced pacemakers firing frequency by approximately15-20%.

these currents are the primary ionic currents regulating the spontaneous firing of pacemaker cells in A. leptorhynchis, and that they are potential targets of steroid action.

the pacemaker rhythm is determined by the interaction of a sodium current that is activated by membrane depolarization, a potassium current that is activated upon depolarization and deactivated during repolarization, and a calcium current that is activated and deactivated during depolarization and repolarization, respectively.
the pharmacological profiles of ionic currents in Pn neurons are similar to those found in other spontaneously firing neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pacemaker rhythm of Pn neurons is generated by a TTX- and 4AP-sensitive current that is modulated by a muO-conotoxins MrVIA- and kappaA conotoxins SIVA-sensitive current and a T-type calcium current.
the pacemaker frequency in the Pn neurons is regulated by a complex interaction of at least three ictonic currents.

TTX, muO-conotoxins, 4AP, kappaA-conotoxins and calcium blockers are all useful tools for studying the pacemaker activity of the medullary nucleus of A. leptorhynchuses, which is a model system for studying neural oscillators and the effects of steroid hormones on neural circuits.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the pacemaker circuitry of Pn neurons in A. leptorhynchu s is remarkably similar to other neural circuits that generate spontaneous oscillations, such as those in the thalamus, hippocampus, and cerebellum, and the pacemaker rhythm is regulated by a similar set of currents in these different circuits.
